<section class="research-intro">
  <div class="research-intro-copy">
    <div class="research-kicker">History of Buddhist art · East Asia</div>
    <h2>Images, rituals, power, and circulation</h2>
    <p>My research examines transformations in Buddhist art over the longue durée, from antiquity to the contemporary period, across China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. I study images and monuments not as isolated objects, but through their patrons, ritual uses, movements, and the political, social, and religious contexts in which they acquire meaning.</p>
    <nav class="research-nav" aria-label="Navigation among research themes">

    <div class="research-node n3">Gender</div>

<section class="research-section" id="axes">

    <div>

      <h2>A social, material, and transregional history of Buddhism</h2>
    </div>
    <p>The different corpora are approached through their inscriptions, materiality, ritual practices, patronage networks, and the circulation of forms among East Asian societies.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="axes-grid">

      </div>
      <div class="axis-copy">
        <div class="axis-number">THEME 01</div>
        <h3>Court Buddhist art and the Koryŏ–Chosŏn transition</h3>
        <p>Artistic continuities beyond dynastic rupture, royal patrons, the role of court women, inscriptions, religious policies, and image production from late Koryŏ to early Chosŏn.</p>
        <div class="axis-tags"><span>Royal court</span><span>Patrons</span><span>Inscriptions</span></div>

      </div>
      <div class="axis-copy">

        <h3>Images, rituals, and performativity</h3>
        <p>The Buddhist image is studied as an object activated through ritual practices and dispositifs. Sweet Dew paintings 甘露圖 provide a particularly rich field for analyzing the emergence, function, and performativity of images.</p>
        <div class="axis-tags"><span>甘露圖</span><span>Rituals</span><span>Performativity</span></div>

        <h3>Architecture, monasteries, and stupas</h3>
        <p>The evolution and persistence of architectural forms, the siting of monasteries, and the history of stupas. The corpora distinguish Silla, Paekche, Koguryŏ, Grand Silla, Koryŏ, and Chosŏn, as well as the different functions of monuments.</p>
        <div class="axis-tags"><span>Stupas</span><span>Monasteries</span><span>Longue durée</span></div>

        <h3>Iconography, death, and salvation</h3>
        <p>Study of the Ten Kings 十王, the Buddhist afterlife, Avalokiteśvara, and processes of local adaptation of iconographic models. This research notably connects Korean and Vietnamese traditions.</p>
        <div class="axis-tags"><span>十王</span><span>Afterlife</span><span>Korea–Vietnam</span></div>

<section class="research-section" id="queer">
  <div class="queer-feature">
    <div class="queer-copy">
      <div class="research-section-kicker">Cross-cutting theme · contemporary period</div>
      <h2>Queer and contemporary Buddhism</h2>
      <p class="artist-name">Pak Kurim 박그림 · Grim Park</p>
      <p>Part of my research examines the relationships between Buddhism, contemporary art, gender, and queer identities in Korea. I am particularly interested in the work of Pak Kurim 박그림, who reworks the techniques and visual structures of Korean Buddhist painting to question identity, gender norms, and binary categories.</p>
      <p>His <em>Shimhodo</em> 尋虎圖 series reinterprets the images of the ox-herding quest, <em>Simudo</em> 尋牛圖, by replacing the ox with the figure of the tiger. Transforming a traditional religious narrative into a contemporary language makes it possible to examine marginality, subjectivity, and the possibility of a queer iconography within inherited forms at the same time.</p>
      <div class="queer-sources"><a class="queer-source" href="https://heypop.kr/n/26670/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Heypop ↗</a><span> · </span><a class="queer-source" href="https://kiaf.org/insights/46599" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Kiaf Seoul ↗</a></div>
    </div>

      <h2>Studying the work within its network</h2>
      <p>My approach combines art history, textual studies, epigraphy, material analysis, social history, fieldwork, and digital tools. The object is not merely described: it is situated within the network of relationships that determine its production, ritual activation, circulation, and reception.</p>
    </div>
